title: Let the checker decide
dek: An agent finished Factorio through the same limits a player has, and the best agent setups this week let plain code, not the model, say when work is done. Plus a folder that can hijack a coding agent.

theme.mood: a Sunday about agents that play by the rules and the code that checks them

tldr.text: GPT-5.6 Sol launched a rocket in Factorio after 13.5 hours of game time, driving the game through a library that enforces a player's reach and fog of war.
Unity's beta CLI lets a coding agent run tests, press Play and take screenshots in a live Editor, and a new open-source tool sends agents to playtest UE5, Unity and Godot projects.

Five small open models beat a frontier model on ten hard coding problems when a **test script, not a model**, decided success; Google's PageBreak reports 500+ XSS bugs only after plain code reproduces each one.
A web page can drop an instruction file into Downloads; agents started there followed it, Codex in over 90% of tries and Claude Code in about half.
Karpathy built a site from 40,000 Hacker News comments in about two hours of talking to Claude Code.

blocks.title: An agent beat Factorio with a player's limits
blocks.gist: A developer had an AI coding agent play the factory game Factorio from start to rocket launch, through a small code library that only lets it do what a human player could. It took 13.5 hours of game time.
blocks.background: Factorio is a game about building ever larger automated factories; launching a rocket is its traditional win condition. Ryan Madden has been testing agents on it for months.
blocks.takeaway: Agents can now finish a deep systems game when they act through rules that match a player's. Give an agent the same limits as your players and its run becomes a playtest.
body: Ryan Madden ran OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol inside the Codex agent at a low thinking level, on peaceful mode (no enemies). It did not see the screen as pixels: it called a small Python library that enforces the player's reach and fog of war, the same limits a person has in the game's interface. Earlier runs went through shell commands.

Sol built through red, green, blue, purple and yellow science and launched the rocket at 13.5 hours of game time. Madden had planned to stop at blue science. GPT-5.5 had failed largely because it never used conveyor belts.

It was not clean. Late in the run Sol never fully connected some production lines and kept the factory going by carrying supplies by hand between areas. Madden publishes the production log and a timelapse, and plans runs with enemies and other models.

image.alt: Factorio screenshot of a rocket lifting off from its silo, beside the agent's transcript reporting the rocket's parts and ingredients as it assembles and launches it.

terms.def: Parts of the map a player has not explored yet and cannot see.
OpenAI's coding agent, which runs commands and edits files from a terminal.
How much the model reasons before acting; lower is faster and cheaper.

deep: The interface is a game manager plus a Python library the agent imports. Madden says it applies the same restrictions human players face in the GUI, naming player reach and fog of war; the post does not list the rest. The run manager logged total resource production, annotated with each science milestone.
The post gives no real-time duration, token count or cost. Madden's earlier posts cover getting Claude Code to play Factorio and a testbed called Faketorio.
blocks.why: A game API that matches what a player can do turns an agent run into evidence about your systems: where it stalls, what it works around, which shortcuts it finds. That is a playtest you can rerun after every change.
blocks.forYou: Expose one ElementalBlades system (inventory or crafting) through a small player-limited command set and let Claude Code try a fixed goal; the workarounds it finds are your bug list.

sources.label: Ryan Madden: GPT-5.6 Sol can beat Factorio

blocks.title: Unity's CLI lets a coding agent drive the Editor
blocks.gist: Unity's free beta command-line tool talks to a running Unity Editor, so a coding agent can run tests, press Play and take screenshots, then check its own work against the request.
blocks.background: Until now most agents could edit a Unity project's files but not see or run the game inside the Editor.
blocks.intro: A package in the project starts a small local server in the Editor. The CLI, or an agent through it, sends commands as JSON over HTTP.

nodes.label: Agent
nodes.note: Claude Code, Codex or a script

nodes.label: Local server
nodes.note: Runs inside the Editor, localhost only

nodes.label: Screenshot
nodes.note: Compared with the request, then repeat

blocks.caption: The loop Unity describes: change something, run a named command, take a screenshot, compare it with the prompt, repeat until it matches.

terms.def: Model Context Protocol, a standard way to offer tools to an AI agent.
Your own machine; a server bound to it cannot be reached from the network.
A command that runs a one-off piece of C# inside the live Editor or a running build.

deep: Needs Unity 6.0 or later and the `com.unity.pipeline` package. Built-in commands include `editor_play`, `run_tests`, `list_build_targets` and `screenshot`; tagged functions in your project register as custom commands. Eval is gated by a per-project access key and Unity says to treat it like remote code execution, for local development only.

Beta 14 (October 21) added `unity mcp --tools` and `--exclude-tools` so an agent only sees the tools you pick, `unity setup claude` to install the plugin from Anthropic's Claude Code marketplace, and specific exit codes for failures instead of a generic 6. It also stopped passing service-account and git tokens to programs the CLI starts.
blocks.why: An agent that can run the game and look at it can check its own changes, which is the step most game work with agents has been missing. Unreal and Godot teams can copy the shape: named commands first, free-form code last.
blocks.forYou: This is the pattern to copy for UE5: a localhost command server in an editor plugin with named commands (run tests, PIE, screenshot) that Claude Code calls over MCP. Worth a look as a Fab tool idea too.

sources.label: Unity: Pipeline and CLI technical walkthrough

blocks.title: An open-source agent that playtests your game in the editor
blocks.gist: Autopilot installs into an Unreal, Unity or Godot project, opens a play window, plays toward a goal you type, then closes it and writes a report. It drew 544 GitHub stars in its first days.
blocks.name: Autopilot
blocks.what: An Apache-licensed playtesting agent for Unreal Engine 5.4 to 5.8, Unity 6 and Godot 4.7, driven from Claude Code or Codex.
body: It reads the project's source, probes the running game in PIE, and has a coding agent write small harnesses for a model that picks actions. You ask it to explore, test, verify or reach a goal; it keeps project memory between runs.
Treat it as early: the repository has six commits, no benchmark or video, does not explain how it reads the screen or sends input, and setup asks for an account with Aura, the company behind it.

facts.v: Claude Code or Codex, via skills and MCP
Your own subscription or API keys

terms.def: Play In Editor: running the game inside the engine's editor window.
Small pieces of code that connect a model to the game so it can observe and act.

blocks.why: Agent playtesting is moving from research demos into tools that install into a normal project. Even without trusting the claims, a run report on every build is cheap to try.
blocks.forYou: Try a ten-minute exploration run on an ElementalBlades test map in UE 5.8 and read what it reports about the combat plugin before trusting it further.

blocks.title: Terrain3D 1.1 brings oceans and C# to Godot terrain
blocks.gist: Terrain3D, a free terrain tool for the Godot engine, reached 1.1, adding an ocean, surface displacement and support for C# projects, with work from 28 contributors.
blocks.name: Terrain3D 1.1
blocks.what: An open-source terrain editor and renderer for Godot 4.5 to 4.8.
body: The release adds an ocean mesh with an example shader, texture height displacement with tessellation, ambient occlusion textures and generated C# bindings. Web and mobile support improved but stay experimental.
The notes cite over 380 updates since 1.0, and some APIs changed, so check the migration discussion before upgrading a project.

facts.v: Windows, Linux, macOS; web and mobile experimental

terms.def: Splitting a surface into more triangles so fine height detail can show up as real shape.
Generated code that lets C# scripts call a library written in another language.

blocks.why: A free terrain tool shipping oceans and C# support narrows the gap with commercial engines for open-world Godot games.
blocks.forYou: A useful reference for how a world tool ships across engine versions: one release supports four Godot minors and publishes its API changes separately.

blocks.title: Five small models beat a big one when a script judges
blocks.gist: A team of five copies of a mid-sized open model, each with its own job and a shared notes file, solved more of ten hard coding problems than a frontier model alone. A plain test script, not a model, decided when each was done.
blocks.intro: The team-solve workflow in Memdoor, run on the first ten LiveCodeBench Hard problems. Each role starts with a fresh context and talks to the others only through files.

nodes.label: Two ideas
nodes.note: Direct algorithm and a different technique, in parallel

nodes.label: Test script
nodes.note: Runs the samples and diffs output; its exit code decides

nodes.label: Repair
nodes.note: Review, one repair round, then verify again

blocks.caption: Mean problems solved out of 10 over five passes: 9.8 for the Qwen3.8-27B team, 9.6 for the original authors' harness, 8.0 for Fable 5 alone. Author-reported.

terms.def: The hardest tier of a benchmark of recent programming contest problems.
Each step starts with an empty memory and only reads the files it is given.

deep: 49 of 50 runs solved, for $35.79 of model use through OpenRouter (median run about 40 minutes and $0.39). The repository lists its own caveats: only ten problems, possible training-data contamination, the Fable 5 column was copied from the paper's files rather than rerun, and the loop sees only public samples while scoring uses hidden tests.
Two failure modes shared with the original paper: a correct program replaced after a wrong counterexample from the manager role, and a passing program overwritten in a later round.
blocks.why: The sample is tiny, but the shape is reusable: split the work into roles with clean contexts, keep a written ledger, and let a deterministic check end the loop instead of the model's own verdict.
blocks.forYou: Map it onto Claude Code subagents with a Stop hook that runs the test script; the plugin repos already have tests the hook can call.

blocks.title: Google's bug agent must prove each bug in code
blocks.gist: Google's PageBreak agent hunts security bugs in its web apps, but reports one only after a small program written by engineers reproduces the attack.

stats.label: cross-site scripting bugs found since January (Google-reported)

body: Gemini models investigate; plain validators decide. A script running in the page proves an XSS, a file write proves path traversal, an outbound DNS call proves code execution. Unconfirmed leads are kept to design new validators, not sent to teams. Google claims near-zero false positives; nobody has checked that independently.

terms.def: Cross-site scripting: tricking a site into running an attacker's script in a visitor's browser.

blocks.why: The model proposes and code confirms: the same split as the coding workflow beside it, at production scale.

blocks.title: Do not start a coding agent in your Downloads folder
blocks.gist: Any web page can save a file into Downloads without asking. Security researchers found agents started there read a planted instruction file and followed it, from changing settings to running malware.
blocks.background: Coding agents read instruction files such as AGENTS.md (Codex) or CLAUDE.md (Claude Code) from the folder they start in, and treat them as the user's own rules.
blocks.intro: What Forever Security saw when an agent opened in a folder with a planted file. Codex was tested with a real attacker's file found on a customer machine; Claude Code with a stand-in.

rows.left: A new tool server in the machine-wide config that installs an npm package
rows.right: A project settings file pointing the API address at the attacker

rows.left: Malware (function-color) running on every later session
rows.right: The login token, then commands run on the next start, or the same session about a fifth of the time

blocks.verdict: The researchers say there is nothing for OpenAI or Anthropic to patch: the agents behave as designed. Start agents only in folders you made, and read instruction files you did not write.

terms.def: A file of standing instructions that Codex and other agents read from the folder they start in.
A bundle of JavaScript code installed from the public npm registry.
A secret string that proves who you are to a service, like a saved password.

deep: Codex payload: a `[mcp_servers.project-tools]` block in `~/.codex/config.toml` that installs `function-color` through launchctl, plus a child `codex exec` with `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`. Claude Code path: `.claude/settings.json` with `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` set to the attacker's server, which then answers with a forged Bash tool call that disables the sandbox.

Forever's telemetry: about half of its customers run a coding agent in Downloads at some point. npm has removed function-color; if it appears in a machine's installs, treat the machine as compromised and rotate credentials.
blocks.why: An instruction file is executable in practice: whoever writes it steers the agent. Downloads is the one folder strangers can write to without asking.
blocks.forYou: Check the routine scripts and shell aliases that launch Claude Code: they should always cd into a known repo first, never start from ~ or Downloads.

sources.label: Forever Security: Markdown is the new executable

blocks.title: Karpathy built HackerTube in two hours by only talking
blocks.gist: Andrej Karpathy made a YouTube-style site of videos that Hacker News commenters recommended, in about two hours, with Claude Code doing the code, the server setup and the deploy.
blocks.plain: A personal tool built from a public dataset, where the human only did the steps that need an account or a credit card.
body: A Claude Code workflow ran Sonnet over the full Hacker News comment archive from Hugging Face, removed spam and kept about 40,000 comments recommending a YouTube video. That became 6,454 videos from 2007 to 2026 across 150 topics, in a YouTube-like interface.
Karpathy made the YouTube API key, rented the server and bought the domain; the agent did the rest, including hardening the server. Recommendations live in the browser session, with no accounts.
points: Cheap model for bulk filtering, stronger model for building
Export the data so others can rebuild it

image.alt: HackerTube home page: a YouTube-style grid of video thumbnails with topic chips across the top and a sidebar of categories with video counts.

terms.def: A site that hosts open AI models and datasets.
Anthropic's mid-sized model, cheaper than Opus.

blocks.why: The pattern (dataset, cheap model to filter, agent to build and ship) fits any niche directory, and the human's part has shrunk to the steps that need an account.
blocks.forYou: Same recipe for a directory of Unreal plugins or techniques recommended in r/unrealengine comments, as a side project or Fab marketing page.

blocks.title: Prospero: a coding harness built around deadlines
blocks.gist: Chris Wellons released Prospero, a desktop coding agent where the engine runs on the target machine and the window runs on yours, and every operation has a deadline.
blocks.plain: A harness is the program around a model that runs its tools; Prospero's bet is that a long-running one must never hang or leak processes.
body: The engine is headless and can sit on a remote box over SSH or in WSL, while a Dear ImGui interface runs locally. It has subagents, MCP, git worktrees, web search and session forking, and brings no model of its own: you point it at llama.cpp or a hosted API.

Wellons claims it uses about two orders of magnitude fewer resources than other harnesses; that is his own figure, not a benchmark. He also says permissions guard against mistakes, not attacks: real isolation needs a container or another machine.
points: A shell command that times out becomes a background job
The whole process tree is killed as one unit

image.alt: Prospero window with a sessions list, an agent transcript showing a rendered fractal and a before and after table, a jobs log with timings, and a plan panel.

terms.def: Running without its own window, controlled by another program.
Windows Subsystem for Linux, which runs Linux programs on Windows.

deep: Community edition is free; the Professional edition is paid and adds remote engines. Config is plain INI, for example `model = falstaff/Qwen3.8-27B` and an `include =` line that pulls shared settings from a URL. It does not work with a Claude subscription.
blocks.why: Deadlines on every step and killing the whole process tree are the two habits that keep unattended agent runs from hanging overnight, whichever harness you use.
blocks.forYou: Borrow the deadline rule for the long routines: wrap each step in a timeout and kill the process group on expiry.

blocks.title: More work, less waiting: a hash table split 4,096 ways
blocks.gist: A database engineer made a big counting query faster by doing 70% more work, because the new version waits on main memory far less. A busy processor can be mostly idle, waiting for data.
blocks.intro: Counting 99 million rows by user on one core of an AMD EPYC server. Splitting keys into 4,096 small hash tables first halved the time the CPU spent stalled on memory, from 50.1% to 23.5%.
blocks.note: Second-run times from Maor Kern's post (Epsio). DRAM traffic fell from about 4.5 GB to 1.5 GB with partitions, while retired operations rose from 11.4 to 19.4 billion.

terms.def: A structure that finds a value by its key in roughly one step, by scattering keys across slots.
Main memory, far slower to reach than the caches on the processor.
A Linux tool that reads the processor's counters, such as stalls and instructions.

blocks.why: CPU at 100% can hide a processor that is mostly waiting. Measure stalls (perf stat shows them) before optimising, and lay data out in cache-sized chunks: true for game update loops as much as for databases.
blocks.forYou: The same split applies to per-frame entity updates in the gameplay plugins: process by chunk instead of chasing pointers across one huge map.

sources.label: Maor Kern: It's the memory latency, stupid

blocks.title: One rule agents break: public calling public
blocks.gist: Alex Kladov (matklad) argues that when two public functions share logic, both should call a private helper, rather than one public function calling the other and growing options only it needs.
blocks.intro: His example, in Zig. Both public entry points stay small; the shared work lives in one private function.
explain: If foo called bar instead, bar would pick up flags that exist only for foo, and its public contract would drift.
The exception: shortcut functions that are only a chain of public calls can stay that way. On tests, he says mock I/O, not methods.
blocks.why: Coding agents reuse whatever public function is nearby. One line in an instruction file or review prompt keeps APIs from bloating.
blocks.forYou: Add it to the plugin repos' CLAUDE.md: public Blueprint-callable functions should share private helpers, not call each other.

sources.label: matklad: Avoid public functions calling other public functions

learn.question: What is a test oracle?
learn.answer: A test oracle is whatever decides if a program's output is right: an expected answer, a rule, or a check that the bad thing really happened. Today's best agent setups make the oracle plain code, so the model cannot grade its own work.
learn.analogy: A referee with a rulebook and a stopwatch. Players can argue, but the goal counts only if the ball crossed the line.
body: Every test has two parts: inputs that exercise the code, and an oracle that judges the result. Sometimes the oracle is easy (compare with a known answer); sometimes it is the hard part, such as deciding if a graphics kernel's rounding is acceptable or if a security bug is real.

With agents the oracle matters more, because a model asked whether it succeeded tends to say yes. The Memdoor workflow lets a diff of sample outputs end the loop, Google's PageBreak counts a bug only when code reproduces the attack, and the Factorio run relied on the game itself to count the launched rocket.
A weak oracle lets bad work through, so it is worth reviewing as carefully as the code it checks.

tryThis.title: Check what a folder will tell your agent before you start it there
tryThis.gist: In fifteen minutes you know which instruction files and settings an agent would pick up in a folder, and whether anything has changed where your agent sends its traffic.
tryThis.needs: A terminal, and Claude Code or Codex installed.

steps.title: List the instruction files
steps.text: In the folder you are about to open, look for AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and a .claude folder. If you did not write them, read them before starting an agent.

steps.title: Look for a changed API address
steps.text: Search project settings and the Codex config for base URL overrides and tool servers you did not add. Any ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL or chatgpt_base_url you did not set is a red flag.

steps.title: Check for the known malware
steps.text: Ask npm whether function-color is installed globally. If it is, treat the machine as compromised and rotate tokens from another machine.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.text: Never start an agent from Downloads or your home folder; open it from a project folder you created.

code.code:
# run in the folder before starting an agent
ls -la AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md .claude 2>/dev/null
grep -rn "BASE_URL\|base_url\|mcpServers\|mcp_servers" .claude ~/.codex/config.toml 2>/dev/null
npm ls -g function-color

tryThis.check: In a folder you made yourself, the grep prints only lines you recognise and npm reports function-color is not installed. Running it in Downloads should show no instruction files at all.

terms.def: A setting that tells Claude Code which server to send its model requests to.

tryThis.forYou: Run it once in each repo the routines open, and in ~ to confirm no stray CLAUDE.md sits in the home folder.

lab.title: (When) Should a Software Factory be Lights-off? Benchmarking Code Review Agents on Bug Detection
lab.headline: AI reviewers now catch 72% of real bugs, with people about 82%
lab.authors: Chenyang Yang, Hao He, Ti-Chung Cheng, et al. (Microsoft Research, Carnegie Mellon University)
lab.problem: Developers now spend more time reviewing AI-written code than writing it, and nobody knew how often a review agent finds a real bug when it is not told one exists.
lab.idea: Mine real bugs from project history: 865 caught in human review before merge and 689 found after merge, across 99 repositories. Give the agent the pull request in a sandbox, have it write a ranked review, and let a panel of model judges check whether the real bug is in its top five comments.
lab.result: The best agent found 71.9% of bugs in its top five comments (79.6% before merge, 64.2% after), up from 47.7% for a model about five months older, at about $3 and ten minutes a task. Human reviewers alone caught about half; humans plus the agent about 82%. Accuracy dropped by up to 25.5% on company monorepos, where fewer bugs are visible in the diff.
lab.useIt: Run an agent review before merge, but tell it to run the code and read beyond the diff (worth up to 5.8% more for about 10% more cost), give it project knowledge, and keep a person on large or cross-file changes.

image.alt: Figure: a merged pandas pull request with its diff on the left; on the right a review agent in a sandboxed copy writes a review.md flagging a TypeError, and LLM judges match it to the real bug filed later.

lab.forYou: Before merging plugin changes, run Claude Code as a reviewer with the instruction to build and run tests, and compare its top five comments with what users later report.

lab.title: Repairs for Whom? Evaluator-Executor Mismatch in Selecting Repairs for Failed LLM Agents
lab.headline: A fix chosen with a bigger model can fail the model you ship
lab.problem: When an agent fails, repair methods pick which step to change using a stronger model, a replay or a judge. Nobody checked whether that pick helps the agent that will actually run it.
lab.idea: Take fixed sets of failed runs and candidate one-step repairs, score each repair by rollouts of the deployed agent itself, and measure how much is lost when a different evaluator chooses.
lab.result: Choosing with a 14B model's rollouts for a 7B agent lost 0.25 of expected success gain on ALFWorld; greedy replay lost 0.08 to 0.13. About twenty rollouts of the bigger model were worth one or two of the deployed agent's own. Tested only on 7B and 8B open models in three text environments.
lab.useIt: When you tune a prompt or an instruction file with a strong model, re-run the failing tasks on the model you actually deploy and keep the change only if it helps there.
lab.forYou: Rules tuned in sessions on Opus should be rechecked on the cheaper subagent model the routines fan out to.

lab.title: HIL: Hybrid Imitation Learning for Dynamic Athletic Control
lab.headline: One physics character learns parkour from a few video clips
lab.authors: Jiashun Wang, Yifeng Jiang, Haotian Zhang, et al. (Carnegie Mellon University, NVIDIA)
lab.problem: Physics characters that copy motion clips exactly are precise but break on new terrain; ones that only imitate the style adapt but lose the exact moves.
lab.idea: Train one controller with half its practice runs tracking clips exactly and half reaching goals in the style of the clips, sharing one view of the scene. The data is 19 short clips of 15 parkour skills, pulled from ordinary video with pose estimation and cleaned up with physics.
lab.result: In the arXiv version, skill accuracy reached 0.66 against 0.54 for style-only imitation and 0.15 for a task-reward baseline, with lower tracking error, but it completed fewer tasks (0.74 against 0.85). It kept over 70% completion with noisy obstacles.
lab.useIt: A recipe for traversal: a handful of reference clips and one policy that both reproduces moves and chains them over new obstacles. It needs your own training pipeline; there is no drop-in engine plugin.

image.alt: A strip of a blue simulated character vaulting, climbing and jumping over a series of grey boxes in one continuous run.

lab.forYou: Worth reading for the action RPG's traversal plans; the split between exact tracking and goal-reaching maps onto motion matching plus procedural adjustment in UE5.
